fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "From the Ranch to the Shop", "body": "George grew up on a remote British Columbia ranch his father assembled from five smaller ones, a day trip from town, with no electricity and no running water, everyone up at four in the morning and working until they could not see. His father built a shop there, and George says he learned as a young child to fix almost anything, and that he disliked repairing things twice, so he fixed them better than new. As a certified automotive technician he complains that the engineers who design cars never work on them, which is why he designs machines to be easy to repair."}, {"title": "Accidents That Became Products", "body": "George started his own business in 1984 on twenty dollars and says he has never worked for anyone since. His first product came from a mistake, a vacuum line left hooked to the carburetor float bowl on a 1977 Volare that kept giving thirty percent better mileage after he shut the rest of the experiment down. He tells Chance he has usually earned more from the side effects of his research than the main line. When a Brown's Gas machine was quoted at three hundred thousand dollars in the late eighties, he built his own instead, and says it made the same gas on half the electricity."}, {"title": "Six Constituents and a Plasma", "body": "George describes Brown's Gas as six constituents rather than plain hydrogen, two thirds hydrogen to one third oxygen atomically, with the atoms recombining in several ways. One of them is still water but carries extra electrons, which makes a gaseous, negatively charged form he calls a plasma, the fourth state after solid, liquid and gas. Chance ties this back to his own interest in the electric body and daily grounding, and George answers with a brick house: a pile of bricks is not a house until some organizing factor and energy puts each one where it belongs."}, {"title": "The Safety Question and the Machine", "body": "Chance presses on whether inhaling the gas has actually been tested for safety, and George answers with the lower combustion limit: keep hydrogen under about four point seven percent of the intake breath and it will not burn, while the research he follows puts the useful level nearer two percent. He points listeners to the Molecular Hydrogen Institute site and to Tyler LeBaron, who consulted with him as an intern. On the machine itself he describes distilled water top ups, a cleaning every hundred or so hours, a lye electrolyte no stronger than liquid soap that stays behind as a catalyst, and redundancy safety built into every step."}, {"title": "Chance's Case for Nutrition First", "body": "Alone in the room afterwards, Chance makes his own case. He notes that hydrogen is literally the simplest atom there is, and that a proton, an electron and a neutron read to him like a Holy Trinity, one and one and one. He is careful to say he cannot fully advocate the machine without having tried it, and puts his own position plainly: the real solutions are nutritional, and the alchemical great work is getting your own cabinet of chemistry in order. He closes on grounding barefoot in the snow, the Telegram group, his sound healing and oracle card sessions, and vibe as the one thing anybody controls."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Inventor George Wiseman explains Brown's gas, molecular hydrogen, and how the AquaCure works, plus the loss that turned an energy researcher toward health.
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: Covers Brown's gas and how it differs from molecular hydrogen, the electrically expanded water component and its six constituents, hydrogen inhalation versus hydrogen-rich drinking water, the 4.7 percent lower combustion limit and inhalation safety, Tyler LeBaron and the Molecular Hydrogen Institute research, AquaCure setup and maintenance, distilled versus mineralized versus alkaline water, and Wiseman's decades as a self-employed inventor working on carburetor enhancers, water torches, and alternative energy.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "The Sludge That Should Not Exist", "body": "Chance opens the second hour on the sludge that collects inside a Brown's Gas electrolyzer, and George walks through the case that convinced him. A chiropractor's ER 1200 gave up several pounds a year, nineteen pounds over three years, yet the anodes and cathodes still weighed the nineteen pounds they weighed when new, so the metal had not dissolved into it. The sludge carried chromium, iron and nickel in roughly the ratios of the stainless plates, which leaves him at Occam's razor: the water itself is transmuting inside the machine."}, {"title": "New Water and Its Erased Memory", "body": "Burning Brown's Gas in a torch turns hydrogen and oxygen back into water that George calls new, water with its memory wiped, which immediately starts taking on whatever sits near it. He describes Joseph Bender and Norman Wooten filling a bottle with new water beside a mineral bottle on a windowsill, sunlight passing through one into the other, and ten ounces of sediment forming that held every one of those fifty minerals. Vernon Ross found the same sediment building electrolyzers from Brown's Gas Book 2, and George offers the fridge test: new water stored beside orange juice will taste of it."}, {"title": "An Electric Realm That Grows Itself", "body": "Chance brings his conversations with Ben Balderson into the room, asking whether a cyclical electrolysis event in a galvanic universe could pour charge back into this realm and grow new land, the way the Avesta describes gods adding ground for people and grazing animals, and whether that explains mud floods and a buried Gobekli Tepe. George answers from the bottom up: drop far enough through molecular and subatomic structure and nothing solid is left, only energy. Hydrogen, appearing and vanishing in space and making up most of the universe, is what he calls the God molecule, with everything denser forming from it."}, {"title": "What He Learned About Life After Death", "body": "Asked how his inner life has shifted, George describes a childhood lived by sunrise and season on a remote ranch, then the spiritual path he took up alongside his late wife, which left him certain that whatever is him does not end with the body. He recounts five cats gathering around him on a couch as they never had before, and a program he badly needed opening on the computer with nobody at the keyboard. He now thanks her daily, says telepathy and the rest are real capacities people have regressed out of, and states plainly that he is not afraid of dying."}, {"title": "Sound, Light, Frequency, and Free Energy", "body": "Chance describes his tuning fork and aura work, including impressions that arrive before a client has spoken, and George meets him with infrared saunas, Gerald Pollack's EZ gel, and the H3O2 layer George credits with keeping capillaries slippery enough for red blood cells to pass. The AquaCure can be set to a single frequency, 432 or 528, with people reporting different responses to each. He also describes a Reiki session across thousands of miles during which he and his late wife lived the same past life at the same moment, plus a clock running for decades on ambient energy, the Lord's pump, and Ezekiel's wheel."}]

fields.Quotes JSON: [{"text": "I didn't like repairing things more than necessary, so I would usually fix it better than it was new.", "author": "George Wiseman", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/94da8d07-3508-4ea4-9e12-31681150e2e9/GEORGE-WISEMAN.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "Lots of people are feeding me information, and then I kind of sort it out and I disseminate it, so everybody thinks I'm a genius, but really I'm not.", "author": "George Wiseman", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/94da8d07-3508-4ea4-9e12-31681150e2e9/GEORGE-WISEMAN.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "I like to say that the best state of mind is alert and relaxed, but most of us in the West, all caffeinated and under-rested, we're tired and wired.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/aa717e55-9487-4255-a7df-3f8ef10940c4/Chance+Garton+Patreon+Portrait.png?content-type=image%2Fpng"}, {"text": "We spend the first third of our life learning what we know how to do, and then we spend another 20 years kind of building into being effective in life.", "author": "George Wiseman", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/94da8d07-3508-4ea4-9e12-31681150e2e9/GEORGE-WISEMAN.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "I'm 32. I could just retire and sit on a beach somewhere. I'm doing this because it's what's needed to be done.", "author": "George Wiseman", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/94da8d07-3508-4ea4-9e12-31681150e2e9/GEORGE-WISEMAN.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "The universe is energy, so your vibe is the only thing you have any control over, and it's what matters most, and it's what everything around you will reflect.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/aa717e55-9487-4255-a7df-3f8ef10940c4/Chance+Garton+Patreon+Portrait.png?content-type=image%2Fpng"}]
